title: How To Keep Your Students Focused The Last Hour Of The School Day t-hour-of-the-school-day/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin tackles the common problem of declining focus and rising misbehavior in the final hour of the school day, offering three concrete fixes. He recommends a short mid-afternoon break tailored to the class's state—active movement if students have been sitting still, or calming breathing exercises if they're returning wound-up from recess or PE. He stresses leaning heavily on well-practiced end-of-day routines so the close of the day matches the purposeful start of the morning, with the teacher shifting into a largely observational role. Finally, he describes a specific silent, standing dismissal routine designed to end the day calmly and without the chaos common at bell time.
points: The type of mid-afternoon break should match students' state: active movement if they've been sitting, calming breathing exercises if they're wound-up from recess or PE.
A calming breathing sequence is described in detail: standing behind desks, slow inhales through the nose and exhales through the mouth, five to ten repetitions.
End-of-day routines should be well-practiced enough that the teacher's role becomes primarily observational, with minimal talking or guidance needed.
A silent, standing dismissal routine—complete with 30 seconds of quiet and individual eye contact—is offered as a way to end the day calmly.
The teachers who produce the most student progress are distinguished less by charisma than by consistently keeping students on task from morning bell to dismissal.
quotes: So much good, quality instruction is lost in the hour before dismissal.
The truth is, the last hour of the day takes more out of you than the preceding hours put together.
In this case, ask your students to stand silently behind their desks, feet wide and hands behind their backs. Pause a moment and let their breathing regulate naturally.
It’s critically important that you finish the school day—that is, the last several minutes—without chaos, confusion, or misbehavior
Have your end-of-day routine finish with every student standing behind their desk, silent, reflective, backpack looped over shoulders.
They’ve developed the classroom management skills to keep distractions, interruptions, and time-consuming misbehaviors to a scanty, bare minimum.
